traits: White to gray powdery coating on leaf surfaces that can be rubbed off
Leaves yellow, curl or drop when the coating is heavy
Worse in shaded, crowded plantings with still air

copy.what_it_means: A white to gray powdery coating that rubs off the leaves suggests powdery mildew. It is usually cosmetic on established plants, though heavy coating can stunt or drop leaves on susceptible varieties. Better light and air circulation are the main fix; a technician can advise if it keeps returning.
copy.fact: Unlike most fungi, powdery mildew thrives in dry air and can infect leaves without any free water on the surface.

tech_notes: Worse in shade with poor air movement; check for coating on both leaf surfaces and on flower buds in heavy cases. Leaves may yellow, curl or drop when the coating is heavy.

signs: White to gray powdery coating on leaf surfaces that can be rubbed off

required_signature.text: A close-up of the leaf showing the white to gray powdery coating.
elements: White to gray powdery coating on leaf surfaces that can be rubbed off

differentials.difference: Powdery mildew coats the leaf top with white powder; downy mildew on viburnum shows angular spots with grayish growth mainly on the leaf underside.
differentials.next_observation: A photo of both the leaf top and the underside.

differentials.difference: Powdery mildew leaves a white powder that rubs off; spider mite damage shows fine stippling and webbing with no powder.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the leaf surface checking for webbing versus powder.

condition.recovery_note: New growth often looks better within a few weeks once air circulation and light improve.

traits: Angular, yellow to brown spots on the leaf, often with grayish fuzzy growth on the underside
Spots follow the leaf veins, giving them a blocky, angular edge
Heavily spotted leaves may drop, but new growth is usually unaffected

copy.what_it_means: Angular, yellow-brown spots on sweet viburnum with grayish growth underneath are commonly called downy mildew, but look-alike fungi cause the same spots. A photo cannot confirm the exact cause; a technician looks at the pattern. Either way it is usually cosmetic and rarely needs more than better air circulation.
copy.fact: UF/IFAS nursery trials found look-alike fungi causing 'downy mildew' symptoms on viburnum so often that some seasons showed no true downy mildew at all, even though the spots looked classic.

tech_notes: Check the leaf underside for grayish sporulation within the angular spots; overhead irrigation and tight spacing favor it. UF/IFAS 2026 nursery trials found Cercospora, Colletotrichum, Corynespora, Phyllosticta, Phoma and Pestalotiopsis species can all produce near-identical symptoms, so do not assume the causal organism from appearance alone.

review.notes: Whether classic-looking spots are truly Plasmopara viburni versus a look-alike fungus is unresolved (UF/IFAS 2026 Florida nursery trials found several look-alike species and some seasons with no true downy mildew at all), which is moot for the customer now that confirmable_by is technician and copy no longer claims a photo settles it.

signs: Angular, yellow to brown spots on the leaf, often with grayish fuzzy growth on the underside
symptoms: Heavily spotted leaves may drop, but new growth is usually unaffected

required_signature.text: A photo cannot confirm the exact fungus; several look-alike species cause identical spots, so a technician looks at the pattern and plant history.
elements: Angular, yellow to brown spots on the leaf, often with grayish fuzzy growth on the underside

differentials.difference: Downy mildew on viburnum shows angular spots with grayish growth mainly underneath; powdery mildew coats the leaf top with white powder.
differentials.next_observation: A photo of both the leaf top and the underside.

condition.recovery_note: New growth is usually unaffected and often looks normal within a few weeks.

traits: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, often with a yellow halo or concentric rings
Leaf margins burn brown and curl or pucker in advanced cases
Twig and branch dieback in severe or repeated infections

copy.what_it_means: Dark, sunken leaf lesions with a yellow halo or concentric rings can suggest anthracnose, but other fungal leaf spots look nearly identical and a yellow halo does not identify the fungus on its own. A technician checks the pattern, any twig dieback and plant stress before recommending a next step.
copy.fact: Anthracnose spores are sticky and spread mainly by splashing rain or irrigation water, not by wind, which is why it often worsens after a wet stretch.

tech_notes: Spores spread by water splash, not wind; check for twig dieback to gauge severity beyond leaf spotting.

signs: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, often with a yellow halo or concentric rings
symptoms: Twig and branch dieback in severe or repeated infections

required_signature.text: A photo cannot confirm this; a technician distinguishes anthracnose from other fungal leaf spots by the pattern, plant history and any twig dieback present.
elements: Dark, sunken lesions on leaves, often with a yellow halo or concentric rings

differentials.difference: Anthracnose and other fungal leaf spots can look alike; a yellow halo or twig dieback is not exclusive to anthracnose and does not identify it alone.
differentials.next_observation: A technician distinguishes the two from the pattern, plant history and any dieback present.

differentials.difference: Salt injury browns leaf tips and margins, often worse on the side facing onshore wind or salt spray; anthracnose causes scattered lesions with a yellow halo.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo of the whole plant checking whether the burn follows the side facing onshore wind or salt spray.

condition.recovery_note: New growth usually looks better within a few weeks once wet weather passes and dead twigs are pruned out.

traits: Small, round to angular leaf spots, tan to brown with a darker purple-red border
Heavily spotted older leaves may yellow and drop while new growth stays clean
Worse after warm, rainy stretches with wet foliage

copy.what_it_means: Small, round to angular tan or brown spots with a darker border suggest a fungal leaf spot. It is usually cosmetic and limited to older leaves. Avoiding overhead watering and clearing fallen leaves are the main fix; a technician can advise if it keeps returning.
copy.fact: This fungal group includes over a thousand species, most of which only ever infect one or a few closely related plants.

tech_notes: Favored by overhead irrigation and frequent rain; usually limited to older, lower foliage. Heavily spotted older leaves may yellow and drop while new growth stays clean.

signs: Small, round to angular leaf spots, tan to brown with a darker purple-red border

required_signature.text: A close-up of the leaf spots showing the tan to brown center and darker purple-red border.
elements: Small, round to angular leaf spots, tan to brown with a darker purple-red border

differentials.difference: Leaf spot fungi and anthracnose can look alike; dieback is not exclusive to anthracnose and a yellow halo does not identify either one from a photo alone.
differentials.next_observation: A technician distinguishes the two from the pattern, plant history and any dieback present.

differentials.difference: Salt injury browns tips and margins, worse facing onshore wind or spray; leaf spot fungi cause scattered round spots across the leaf, not just the margin.
differentials.next_observation: A wider photo of the whole plant checking whether the burn follows the side facing onshore wind or salt spray.

condition.recovery_note: New growth is usually unaffected; older spotted leaves may drop over a few weeks.

traits: Canopy thins with reduced vigor and twig dieback, often starting on one side of the plant
Leaves yellow and drop, and the plant may wilt despite moist soil
Worse in poorly drained soil or after heavy, frequent watering

copy.what_it_means: A thinning canopy, yellowing leaves and wilting despite moist soil can suggest a root rot, but a photo cannot confirm it. A technician digs at the root crown to check whether the root cortex sloughs off, and checks the drainage before recommending a next step.
copy.fact: Phytophthora is technically not a true fungus; it is a water mold that spreads best through waterlogged soil, which is why drainage matters so much for this disease.

tech_notes: Confirm by checking whether the fibrous root cortex sloughs off the white root core when squeezed; rule out drought and over-mulching first.

review.notes: The root-cortex-sloughing diagnostic description is the most detailed UF/IFAS source found but is written for citrus (HS261), a genus-level Phytophthora trait rather than a woody-ornamental-specific fact sheet; PP123 confirms overwatering as a general catalyst for Phytophthora/Fusarium root and crown disease on ornamentals but does not detail the sloughing symptom itself.

symptoms: Canopy thins with reduced vigor and twig dieback, often starting on one side of the plant
Leaves yellow and drop, and the plant may wilt despite moist soil

required_signature.text: A photo cannot confirm this; a technician digs at the root crown to check whether the root cortex sloughs off the white root core.
elements: Canopy thins with reduced vigor and twig dieback, often starting on one side of the plant

differentials.difference: Transplant shock affects a recently moved plant and often improves within months; root rot can affect an established plant and worsens with wet soil.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks the roots and confirms how recently the plant was planted.

differentials.difference: A buried root flare confirms deep planting, but does not rule out root rot at the same time; a technician checks the roots regardless.
differentials.next_observation: A technician digs at the roots to check for rot even when the flare is visibly buried.

condition.recovery_note: Recovery depends on how much root and trunk tissue is affected and can take months once drainage is corrected.

traits: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling on leaves that does not mirror on both sides of the leaf
Lopsided, small, bitter fruit that stays green at the blossom end while the stem end colors
Individual shoots or branches turn bright yellow

copy.what_it_means: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling and small, lopsided, bitter fruit can suggest citrus greening, a bacterial disease that cannot be cured. A lab test confirms it. Your extension office explains ways to support nearby citrus; removal is the owner's call with a licensed professional.
copy.fact: Citrus greening is spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, a tiny insect that picks up the bacterium from an infected tree and carries it to the next one it feeds on.

tech_notes: Confirmed by PCR through FDACS Division of Plant Industry or the UF/IFAS Plant Diagnostic Center; check for the Asian citrus psyllid on new flush.

review.notes: Owner re-approved 2026-10-02 after the UF/IFAS season check of the yard calendar.

signs: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling on leaves that does not mirror on both sides of the leaf
Lopsided, small, bitter fruit that stays green at the blossom end while the stem end colors
symptoms: Individual shoots or branches turn bright yellow

required_signature.text: A photo of the blotchy mottling or lopsided fruit can raise concern, but only a lab PCR test confirms citrus greening.
elements: Blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling on leaves that does not mirror on both sides of the leaf

differentials.difference: Citrus greening shows blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling and lopsided bitter fruit; citrus canker shows raised, corky lesions with a yellow halo.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up comparing leaf mottling versus raised corky lesions.

differentials.difference: The psyllid is the insect that spreads greening; finding it or its notched nymphs on new shoots shows exposure risk, not confirmed infection.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of new shoot tips checking for the insect, alongside a lab test of the tree.

condition.recovery_note: There is no recovery once a tree is infected; nutrition and irrigation support general tree condition but do not reverse the disease.

traits: Raised, corky lesions with sunken centers and a yellow halo on leaves, fruit and stems
Lesions appear on both sides of the leaf, unlike most leaf spots
Heavily infected leaves and fruit drop early
safety_line: Florida citrus is under a statewide quarantine covering nursery stock and fruit movement; your county extension office handles confirming a suspected case.

copy.what_it_means: Raised, corky lesions with a yellow halo on leaves, fruit and stems can suggest citrus canker, regulated under a statewide quarantine that mainly governs moving citrus nursery stock and fruit, not home-tree removal. A photo alone does not confirm it; your extension office arranges a proper look.
copy.fact: Florida dropped its tree-by-tree citrus canker eradication program in 2006 and moved to a statewide USDA quarantine that regulates how citrus nursery stock and fruit can be moved.

tech_notes: Do not mail samples; contact the local UF/IFAS Extension office to have an agent examine the tree and advise on reporting.

review.notes: Reporting a suspected case through the county extension office is recommended, not a stated legal requirement for homeowners per FDACS's homeowner FAQ, which is why action routes to a specialist referral rather than a reporting mandate.

signs: Raised, corky lesions with sunken centers and a yellow halo on leaves, fruit and stems
symptoms: Lesions appear on both sides of the leaf, unlike most leaf spots

required_signature.text: A photo of raised, corky lesions with a yellow halo can raise concern, but confirmation goes through your county extension office.
elements: Raised, corky lesions with sunken centers and a yellow halo on leaves, fruit and stems

differentials.difference: Citrus canker shows raised, corky lesions with a yellow halo; citrus greening shows blotchy, asymmetrical yellow mottling and lopsided bitter fruit.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up comparing raised corky lesions versus leaf mottling.

condition.recovery_note: Existing lesions do not clear up; your extension office explains what to expect for the tree going forward.

traits: Scalloped yellowing along the leaf margin, followed by browning and scorch at the tip or edge
Scorch starts on one branch and spreads through the canopy over one to two years
Branches die back after their leaves scorch

copy.what_it_means: Scalloped yellowing that spreads into scorch and branch dieback over one to two years can suggest oleander leaf scorch, a bacterial disease that cannot be cured. A lab test confirms it. An arborist can advise on pruning; removal is the owner's call with a licensed professional.
copy.fact: The bacterium behind oleander leaf scorch lives in the plant's water-conducting tissue and is spread by insects, such as spittlebugs and sharpshooters, that feed there.

tech_notes: Prune infected limbs 2-3 feet below visible symptoms on newly infected plants; full removal is typically recommended once most of the canopy is affected.

review.notes: Current establishment/severity of oleander leaf scorch specifically in Sarasota-Charlotte-Manatee-Lee-Collier is not separately confirmed; the UF/IFAS source describes the disease generally for Florida oleander, so range is set to occasional as an estimate.

symptoms: Scalloped yellowing along the leaf margin, followed by browning and scorch at the tip or edge
Scorch starts on one branch and spreads through the canopy over one to two years

required_signature.text: A photo of scalloped yellowing and marginal scorch spreading through the canopy can raise concern, but only a lab test confirms the bacterium.
elements: Scalloped yellowing along the leaf margin, followed by browning and scorch at the tip or edge

differentials.difference: Both can look one-sided in a photo; leaf scorch spreads from one branch over months to years, while salt injury tracks wind or spray exposure.
differentials.next_observation: A technician tracks whether the browning spreads from one branch over time, or tests for the bacterium.

condition.recovery_note: There is no recovery once scorch spreads through the canopy; pruning infected limbs well below the symptoms may slow spread on a newly affected plant.

traits: Sudden wilting, with leaves turning brown but hanging on the branches
Toothpick-like frass or sawdust tubes pushing out of the bark
Dark streaks in the wood when a strip of bark is peeled back
Affects avocado, redbay and swampbay, and can kill a tree within weeks to a few months

copy.what_it_means: A tree that wilts suddenly, with brown leaves that stay attached, can suggest laurel wilt, a fatal disease of avocado, redbay and swampbay. A photo cannot confirm it. This is a report-and-refer case for the county extension office or state plant regulators.
copy.fact: Laurel wilt is carried into trees by the redbay ambrosia beetle, and UF/IFAS lists no approved fungicide that prevents it or stops it in home landscape avocado.

tech_notes: Frass tubes on the trunk and dark streaks under the bark are the field clues; do not diagnose. Refer to the county extension office or FDACS Division of Plant Industry for reporting and confirmation, and note that shot-hole borers and ambrosia beetles are a look-alike for the frass.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). Timing corrected to the source: HS1358 says death can come three weeks to three months after infection, not the 4 to 8 weeks in the owner brief. Not modeled as regulated: HS1358 recommends reporting to DPI or extension but the catalog rule for regulated entries needs owner direction.

signs: Toothpick-like frass or sawdust tubes pushing out of the bark
Dark streaks in the wood under peeled bark
symptoms: Sudden wilting, with brown leaves that stay attached to the branches
A tree in the laurel family (avocado, redbay, swampbay) declining fast

required_signature.text: A photo of sudden wilting with brown leaves that hang on can raise concern, but only lab confirmation identifies laurel wilt; report it and refer.
elements: Sudden wilting, with brown leaves that stay attached to the branches

differentials.difference: Both leave frass on the trunk; laurel wilt adds sudden wilting of the whole tree, while borer damage often shows first as branch dieback.
differentials.next_observation: A wide photo of the whole canopy and a close-up of the frass on the trunk.

condition.recovery_note: There is no recovery once a tree is infected; infected avocado trees usually die within weeks to a few months.

traits: Yellow to dark brown, greasy-looking blotches, first on the underside of mature leaves
Matching yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Heavy leaf drop in late winter to early spring on affected trees

copy.what_it_means: Yellow-brown, greasy-looking blotches and winter leaf drop on citrus can suggest greasy spot, but other citrus leaf problems look alike. A technician checks the pattern and timing; the spores are released in spring and summer, and symptoms follow months later.
copy.fact: Greasy spot has a long delay: spores land in spring and summer, but the spotting only shows up in fall and winter.

tech_notes: Spores are released April to July; symptoms show November to January, and leaves drop in late winter. Time the visit to the spring release window rather than to when the spots appear.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). active_months combine the spore-release months (April-July) with the symptom months (November-January); peak_months [5, 6, 7] follow the owner brief and sit in the spore-release window.

symptoms: Yellow to dark brown, greasy-looking blotches, first on the underside of mature leaves
Matching yellow spots on the upper leaf surface
Leaf drop in late winter to early spring

required_signature.text: A photo of greasy-looking blotches with yellow spots on the upper leaf can raise concern, but a technician distinguishes greasy spot from other citrus leaf problems.
elements: Yellow to dark brown, greasy-looking blotches, first on the underside of mature leaves

differentials.difference: Greasy spot is a greasy-looking blotch on leaves; melanose is sandpaper-rough brown specks on fruit and leaves.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the leaf and of any fruit, checking for rough, sandpaper-like specks.

differentials.difference: Rust mites bronze the fruit rind; greasy spot marks the leaves with greasy blotches and drops them in winter.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of a leaf and of the fruit rind on the same tree.

condition.recovery_note: Trees usually keep growing after leaf drop, but timing matters; plan around the spring spore window rather than the winter symptoms.

traits: Sandpaper-rough brown specks on fruit and leaves
Specks may form streaks or tear-drop patterns on fruit
Dead twigs and dead wood in the canopy nearby

copy.what_it_means: Sandpaper-rough brown specks on citrus fruit and leaves can suggest melanose, which mostly affects how the fruit looks. A technician checks the pattern and the canopy, because dead wood is where the spores come from.
copy.fact: The melanose fungus grows on dead twigs in the tree, so the specks on fruit and leaves trace back to dead wood in the canopy, not to the fruit itself.

tech_notes: Dead twigs (roughly 1/8 to 1/4 inch) that died within recent months are the spore source; prune dead wood and dispose of brush piles promptly. Infection risk depends on fruit size and wet spring weather.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). Source is the commercial citrus production guide (spring infection window around fruit set); months [3-7] and peak [4, 5, 6] follow the owner brief and match its April start of protection.

verification.claim: Streak or tear-drop pattern on fruit
verification.note: Common melanose description not stated in the excerpted CG019 text; confirm at review.

signs: Sandpaper-rough brown specks on fruit and leaves
symptoms: Dead twigs and dead wood in the canopy nearby

required_signature.text: A photo of sandpaper-rough brown specks can raise concern, but a technician confirms melanose by the pattern and the dead wood in the canopy.
elements: Sandpaper-rough brown specks on fruit and leaves

differentials.difference: Melanose is sandpaper-rough brown specks on fruit and leaves; greasy spot is a greasy-looking blotch on leaves with winter leaf drop.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the leaf and of any fruit, checking for rough, sandpaper-like specks.

differentials.difference: Rust mite bronzes the fruit rind smoothly or with a sharkskin look; melanose leaves distinct sandpaper-rough brown specks.
differentials.next_observation: A close-up of the rind, plus a photo of dead twigs in the canopy.

condition.recovery_note: The specks on existing fruit do not fade, but removing dead wood lowers pressure on new growth over the following season.
